title: Priya and the Crumbling Ball
markdown:
Sunbeams blasted through Priya’s window. A zappy energy buzzed. She jumped up. Today was the test for her super-bouncy blue ball. She dashed to the workbench. Rune, her smart crow, swooped in and landed on the lamp as if he had booked the seat.

No. The ball sat lifeless. It flopped. Priya’s shoulders sagged. Rune cawed, a sound that meant I told you not to leave chemistry overnight.

“It’s broken.” She tapped it. A crumbly bit broke off and powdered her palm. “Yesterday it bounced. Now it’s sad and brittle. What happened?”

She grabbed the remains and bolted outside, Rune close behind. “Inventor Imani. Help.”

Imani’s workshop blasted with gears and sparks. A yummy smell — something baking that was probably not meant to be eaten — filled the air. Imani grinned. “Priya. Rune. What’s up?”

Priya presented the droopy ball. “Easily broken. Won’t bounce. Why?”

Imani’s eyes sparkled. “Maybe something mixed with the stuff it’s made of. Everything is tiny bits that stick. Different kinds of hold.”

She tossed a pinch of salt. It exploded into dust. “See how fast it breaks? These bits lock tight. A hold that can be brittle. Super glue that crumbles.”

Next, a sugar cube. “These bits share little pieces with each other. A sharing hold. Strong, and sometimes bendy — closer to what your ball used to be.” She tapped the cube into water. It melted, a quiet surrender.

Then metal, a scrap from the bench. “A happy crowd, jiggling, electrons free to wander. A wiggly hold. That’s why metal can take a knock.”

Priya’s eyes went wide. “Salt: tight and breakable. Sugar: sharing and bendy. Metal: a dance party that doesn’t snap.”

“The kind of hold decides everything. Your ball had bendy sharing holds that stretched and sprang back. Something changed them.”

Rune tapped the sad ball, then flapped toward Priya’s workbench. She gasped. “Yesterday I tried a new coating. Some spilled near the ball. Smelled sharp.”

They raced back. A faint smudge still tingled in the air, the ghost of a solvent that had no business near a polymer. Imani sniffed, then did not sniff again. “That sharp smell could have loosened the sharing holds. Messed the network. Brittle instead of springy.”

Priya looked at the dull ball. The bounce was gone because how its tiny bits held together had changed. She did not announce that the world was a wonderful experiment. She bagged the crumbled coating, labelled the solvent so she would not ‘just try a smear’ again, and set the salt, sugar, and metal scrap in a row as a reminder of three different holds.

Imani smiled without calling anyone clever. “You know why it failed. That’s the useful part.”

Priya picked up the sad ball. It would not bounce today. A spark still flashed — not a declaration. She mixed a fresh batch on a clean corner of the bench, Rune supervising from the lamp, and left the ruined sphere in a jar marked do not bounce, learn from.
